lesson.title: Capstone: The Bridge Reading
lesson.subtitle: Ein Tag in Berlin — one connected story built from everything you own

hook.title: The Bridge
hook.content: Ninety lessons ago you learned that Brücke means bridge. Today you cross it. Below is a connected story — 'Ein Tag in Berlin' — built almost entirely from words you have met, annotated with the shifts that explain them, and seeded with the false friends lying in wait. Every sentence is a sentence you can now decode, and most of them you can build. Read it twice: once for the story, once for the machinery. Then the exercises hand you the pen.

footnotes.title: The Reading Passage
footnotes.content: Der Mann und die Frau wohnen in Berlin. Gestern hatten? — gestern machten sie? keep it Perfekt: Gestern haben sie eine Fahrt mit dem Zug gemacht. Der Zug war schnell. In der Stadt haben sie Brot und Wasser gekauft. Am Abend hat der Mann ein Buch gelesen, und die Frau hat? — die Kinder? die Frau hat das Licht angemacht? — fine: und die Frau hat gelacht. Um elf Uhr? — Um elf war die Nacht still, und das Haus war dunkel. Heute trinken sie Kaffee. Es gibt keinen besseren Morgen — there is no better morning.

pattern.title: Decode, Then Predict
pattern.content: Decode pass: every capital word carries a shift receipt (Zug pulls, Fahrt fares, Nacht keeps its ch). Grammar pass: the Perfekt brackets (haben...gekauft), the dative receivers, the V2 walls, the subclause basements. Prediction pass: cover the German and rebuild it from the English — then reverse. The false friends are hiding: Rat is advice, fast is almost, bald is soon. When you can read this passage and rebuild its sentences, the trail is behind you and German is ahead.
pattern.linguist_note: The passage is deliberately short — about sixty words — because density, not length, is the test: nearly every word in it has appeared in a lesson table, and every construction has been drilled.

exercises.prompt: Reading check — match each story sentence with its English meaning:

matching_pairs.english: Yesterday they took a trip by train
matching_pairs.german: Gestern haben sie eine Fahrt mit dem Zug gemacht

matching_pairs.english: In the city they bought bread and water
matching_pairs.german: In der Stadt haben sie Brot und Wasser gekauft

matching_pairs.english: At eleven the night was still
matching_pairs.german: Um elf war die Nacht still

matching_pairs.english: The market is at the river
The picture hangs on the wall
matching_pairs.german: Das Bild hängt an der Wand

matching_pairs.english: They look out of the window

exercises.target_answer: Gestern haben sie eine Fahrt mit dem Zug gemacht, Der Zug war schnell, In der Stadt haben sie Brot und Wasser gekauft, Um elf war die Nacht still, Es ging ihm übel, Die Kinder ziehen sich aus, Der Markt ist am Fluss, Das Bild hängt an der Wand, Sie wollte gewinnen, Sie schauen aus dem Fenster
exercises.meaning: the story beats of the passage
exercises.explanation: Perfekt brackets, sein-pasts, and dative time — every construction from the trail, in one story.

exercises.prompt: Trap watch: in the story's world, someone asks for 'Rat'. What do they get?
exercises.explanation: The false-friend deck strikes: der Rat is advice. The rodent is die Ratte. The bait 'a gift' is die Gabe — the giving that es gibt names.

exercises.prompt: 'Das Haus war dunkel' — which decode runs through 'dunkel'?
exercises.explanation: One of the trail's first shifts closes the capstone: the d-words answer to English th.

exercises.prompt: The story's morning line hides a shift family: 'Morgen' is the twin of which English word?
exercises.explanation: The very first sprig taught you this pair — the bridge begins and ends with twins.

exercises.idea: you're closing your Berlin story at dawn: there is no better morning
cues: es gibt (existence by giving) + keinen (no, Him-Case) + besseren (better with its ending) — four lessons in five words
exercises.explanation: es gibt (existence by giving) + keinen (negated accusative) + besseren (the comparative with its ending) — four lessons in five words. The story's own adjectives close the loop: das Essen war fertig, die Leute waren lustig, und das Wetter war schlecht.

summary.outcome: Read and rebuild a connected German story using the entire trail.
summary.takeaway: You crossed the bridge: sixty words, every one decoded by a law you own — the trail ends, the language begins.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: A Day in Berlin, the full reading — with tap-to-inspect words and shift annotations.

twist.prompt: Doubt the ending: there is no better morning → IS there no better morning? (The verb flips, es follows.)
twist.explanation: In the question, gibt takes position 1 and es falls in behind — the ancient flip, one last time. The capstone closes where the trail began: the verb knows its seat.

mann.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *mann- — the identical twin of man; German keeps the short a English lengthened. [wiktionary]

frau.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ 'lady, mistress' — kin to archaic English frow 'lady'; Fräulein andMs.-style Frauennamen carry the same root. [wiktionary]

kind.context_translation: The child plays in the garden.
kind.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kindą, related to the root of English kin — 'of the family'. The t → z shift never fired here; the d hardened to t instead. [wiktionary]

zug.etymology_derivation: Noun of ziehen (to pull — the tow/tug family): a train is 'the pull(er)', an elevator the Aufzug ('up-pull'). [wiktionary]

fahrt.etymology_derivation: Noun of fahren (fare): a 'faring' — a drive, ride, or voyage; the -t is the Germanic -þ nominal suffix. [wiktionary]

kaufen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kaupōną, borrowed from Latin caupō 'tradesman/innkeeper' — the same loan that gave English cheap; collateral cognates. [wiktionary]

brot.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *braudą — originally "the fermented/risen thing", kin to the verb brew (German brauen). Bread is "the brewed thing". [wiktionary]

buch.context_translation: I am reading a good book.

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

morgen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English morrow (hence to-morrow) and morn — both descend from the Germanic root for "morning". [wiktionary]

nacht.context_phrase: In der Nacht ist es hier sehr ruhig.
nacht.context_translation: At night it is very quiet here.

gabe.etymology_derivation: geben frozen into a noun — the true twin of English gift ('a giving'); verb and noun shared by both languages. [wiktionary]

schlecht.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *slihtaz 'smooth, level' — Wiktionary: cognate with English slight. [wiktionary]

fertig.etymology_derivation: From Old High German fartig, literally journey-ready, from fart (journey), the ancestor of modern Fahrt; the root belongs with the Germanic travel word behind English fare, and Dutch has the parallel vaardig. [wiktionary]

lustig.etymology_derivation: Lust (desire, joy) plus -ig; Lust is the exact cognate of English lust, from Proto-Germanic *lustuz, though in German the sexual shade is weak and the word still means plain pleasure, as in Lust haben. [wiktionary]

übel.context_translation: I feel a bit sick today.
übel.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *ubil — English evil is the documented cognate; both descend from the same ancient word for bad. [wiktionary]

fluss.context_phrase: Der Fluss fließt durch die Stadt.
fluss.context_translation: The river flows through the city.
fluss.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German vluȥ, from Proto-Germanic *flutiz, from the same root as fließen, to flow. English flow is the cognate of that root. [wiktionary]

markt.context_phrase: Auf dem Markt kaufe ich Obst.
markt.context_translation: At the market I buy fruit.
markt.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *markat, an early Latin borrowing shared with English market. [wiktionary]

wand.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wanduz 'fence' — Wiktionary: cognate with English wand, not wall. [wiktionary]

gewinnen.context_phrase: Unser Team will das Spiel gewinnen.
gewinnen.context_translation: Our team wants to win the game.
gewinnen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *winnaną (PIE *wenh₁-) — English win descends from the same root (Old English winnan); strong verb: gewann, gewonnen. [wiktionary]

schauen.context_phrase: Wir schauen das Spiel im Fernsehen.
schauen.context_translation: We watch the game on TV.
schauen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *skawwōną (to look); the page cites Old English scēawian and compares English show — the old look-verb that English turned into show. [wiktionary]

ausziehen.english_cognate: to take off, to move out
ausziehen.english_meaning: to take off, to move out
ausziehen.context_phrase: Zuhause ziehe ich die Schuhe aus.
ausziehen.context_translation: At home I take off my shoes.
ausziehen.etymology_derivation: aus (out) + ziehen (to pull): aus is the t-to-s twin of English out, and the root is the *teuhaną of English tug. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
